latest_nl_proof:
Let
A = { b in {2,...,p-1} : I(b) + b > p + 2 }.
I will show first that |S| = |A|, and then count A.

First note that I is an involution: for every x in {1,...,p-1}, both x and I(I(x)) are inverses of I(x) modulo p, so by uniqueness I(I(x)) = x. In particular I is a permutation of {1,...,p-1}. Also I(x) = x implies x^2 ≡ 1 (mod p), hence (x-1)(x+1) ≡ 0 (mod p); since p is prime, the only fixed points are x = 1 and x = p-1.

Now define
phi(k) = I(k) + 1  for k in {1,...,p-2}.
Because I is a permutation and the unique preimage of p-1 is p-1 itself, we have I(k) in {1,...,p-2} for k in {1,...,p-2}; hence phi is a bijection from {1,...,p-2} onto {2,...,p-1}.

Take k in {1,...,p-2}, and set b = phi(k) = I(k)+1. In the field F_p we have
b (p+1-I(k+1)) ≡ (I(k)+1)(1-I(k+1))
≡ (k^{-1}+1)(1-(k+1)^{-1})
= ((k+1)/k)·(k/(k+1))
≡ 1 (mod p).
Since k+1 is in {2,...,p-1}, we have I(k+1) != 1, so p+1-I(k+1) lies in {1,...,p-1}. By uniqueness of the representative inverse, this shows
I(b) = p + 1 - I(k+1).
Therefore
k in S
iff I(k+1) < I(k)
iff p+1-I(k+1) > p+1-I(k)
iff I(b) > p+1-I(k).
But b = I(k)+1, so p+1-I(k) = p+2-b. Hence
k in S iff I(b) > p+2-b iff b in A.
Thus phi restricts to a bijection S -> A, and therefore
|S| = |A|.

So it remains to count A.

The non-fixed points of the involution I split into unordered 2-cycles {u,v} with 1 <= u < v <= p-1 and uv ≡ 1 (mod p). Since the only fixed points are 1 and p-1, the number of such 2-cycles is
T = (p-3)/2.
For such a cycle {u,v}, put sigma = u+v. Then both members of the cycle have the same value x+I(x), namely sigma. Hence this 2-cycle contributes 2 elements to A exactly when sigma > p+2, and contributes 0 otherwise. Also p-1 belongs to A because (p-1)+I(p-1)=2p-2 > p+2, while 1 does not belong to A because 1+I(1)=2.

Let H be the number of 2-cycles {u,v} with u+v > p+2. Then
|A| = 1 + 2H.

Now consider the map on 2-cycles
{u,v} -> {p-v, p-u}.
Because (p-u)(p-v) ≡ uv ≡ 1 (mod p), this is again a 2-cycle for I. Its sum is
(p-v) + (p-u) = 2p - (u+v).
So this map bijects the 2-cycles with sum < p-2 and the 2-cycles with sum > p+2.

There are no 2-cycles with sum p+2 or p-2:
- If u+v = p+2, then v ≡ 2-u (mod p), so
  1 ≡ uv ≡ u(2-u) (mod p),
  hence u^2 - 2u + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p), i.e. (u-1)^2 ≡ 0 (mod p). Thus u = 1, which would force v = p+1, impossible.
- If u+v = p-2, then v ≡ -2-u (mod p), so
  1 ≡ uv ≡ -u(u+2) (mod p),
  hence u^2 + 2u + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p), i.e. (u+1)^2 ≡ 0 (mod p). Thus u = p-1, which would force v = -1, impossible.

Therefore the only cycle sums not paired off by the above bijection are p-1, p, and p+1.
Let M be the number of 2-cycles whose sum lies in {p-1, p, p+1}. Then
T = 2H + M.
Also M <= 3, because for each fixed integer s in {p-1,p,p+1}, a 2-cycle {u,v} with u+v=s gives the two roots of the quadratic congruence
x^2 - s x + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p),
and a quadratic over F_p has at most two roots, so there is at most one unordered pair for each such s.

Hence
|S| = |A| = 1 + 2H = 1 + T - M
>= 1 + (p-3)/2 - 3
= (p-7)/2.

Finally, since p > 5 and p ≡ 5 (mod 8), we have p >= 13. Therefore
(p-7)/2 >= (p-1)/4 = floor(p/4).
So
|S| >= floor(p/4),
as required.
role_in_parent: Covers one of the residue classes that the last failed attempt explicitly omitted; this repairs the missing-coverage defect.
statement_nl: Let p be a prime number with p > 5 and p ≡ 5 (mod 8). For each k in {1,2,...,p-1}, let I(k) be the unique integer in {1,2,...,p-1} such that k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p), and define S = { k in {1,2,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }. Then |S| >= floor(p/4).

domain_restrictions: p must be prime (so inversion mod p exists for all k ∈ {1,...,p-1})
k are integers restricted to {1,...,p-1} when defining I and to {1,...,p-2} when testing the inequality
I(k) is taken as the representative of the multiplicative inverse in the set {1,...,p-1}
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every prime p with p > 5 and p ≡ 5 (mod 8), define the function I : {1,...,p-1} → {1,...,p-1} by I(k) being the unique integer in {1,...,p-1} with k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p). Let S = { k ∈ {1,...,p-2} | I(k+1) < I(k) }. Then the cardinality of S satisfies |S| ≥ floor(p/4). (Equivalently, since p ≡ 5 (mod 8), |S| ≥ (p-1)/4.)
quantifier_order: ∀ p: p is an integer prime, with p > 5 and p ≡ 5 (mod 8)
(definition) ∀ k ∈ {1,...,p-1}, I(k) is the (unique) integer in {1,...,p-1} satisfying k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p)

variables.domain: p is a prime number, p > 5, and p ≡ 5 (mod 8)
variables.name: p
variables.role: parameter (quantified universally over primes with the given properties)

variables.domain: for each p, k ranges over {1,2,...,p-1} when defining I(k); in the set S, k ranges over {1,2,...,p-2}
variables.name: k

variables.domain: I : {1,...,p-1} -> {1,...,p-1}, defined by the modular inverse relation k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p)
variables.name: I
variables.role: defined witness mapping (unique multiplicative inverse mod p for each k)

variables.name: S
variables.role: derived set whose cardinality is being bounded

witness_dependencies: I(k) depends on both p and k: I = I_p with I_p(k) the unique inverse of k modulo p in {1,...,p-1}
S depends on p (via the function I defined modulo p)
The numeric bound floor(p/4) depends on p; for p ≡ 5 (mod 8) this equals (p-1)/4 (an integer)
